summary: We developed Astrobot: Nova Mission, a 2D interactive simulator of space exploration and orbital operations built with HTML5 Canvas and JavaScript, set aboard a space station en route to the exoplanet Kepler-186f.   The project addresses the challenge of making aerospace engineering and astronomy accessible to the public through a hands-on five-day orbital campaign. Players control Astrobot to diagnose systems, gather hardware components, resolve life support emergencies (O2 and H2O), and calibrate 20 real physical parameters—such as cabin pressure, satellite telemetry, and propulsion—before configuring and launching the Nova Probe under realistic budget and mass constraints. It also features an interactive astronomical scanner, bilingual support (Spanish/English), and dedicated controls for both PC and mobile devices.   This tool is important because it democratizes STEM education and inspires scientific careers using open web technologies that require no installation, demonstrating how exploring potentially habitable worlds demands technical precision, critical thinking, and efficient resource management.
details:
What exactly does it do?

Astrobot: Nova Mission is a 2D interactive simulator of space exploration and orbital operations set on a space station en route to Kepler-186f, the first Earth-sized exoplanet discovered in the habitable zone of a red dwarf star.

The player controls Astrobot, an autonomous maintenance robot, throughout a five-day orbital campaign, exploring six interconnected modules of the station (Central Corridor, Bridge, Workshop and Propulsion, Science Lab, Storage and Logistics, and Crew Quarters) and interacting with nine crew members and the artificial intelligence ORION-7. The simulator integrates four main dynamics:

  • Solving 20 Engineering and Science Missions (Days 1–4): Troubleshooting, locating hardware components (such as LiOH scrubber cartridges, cryptographic keys, or pyrotechnic valves), and calibrating real aerospace systems.
  • Life Support and Emergency Management: Continuous monitoring of oxygen reserves (O2), water consumption (H2O) in electrolysis processes, and resolving critical emergencies with a 60-second countdown.
  • Interactive Astronomical Observation: Four panoramic windows equipped with a space scanner that identifies and displays scientific data about Kepler-186f, Saturn and its moons (Titan, Enceladus, and Mimas), Proxima Centauri, and the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), as well as hidden science fiction references.
  • Assembly and Orbital Launch (Day 5): After progressively constructing the Nova Probe in the cargo bay over the first four days, the player configures the launch vehicle, power system, and science payload under realistic budget constraints ($100M maximum) and mass capacity limitations to successfully deploy the probe.

How does it work?

The project is built on a lightweight, single-file web architecture that runs a continuous simulation loop at 60 frames per second (requestAnimationFrame) directly in the browser:

  • 100% Procedural Graphics Rendering: Instead of downloading external images, all characters, animations, lighting, shooting stars, planets, and machinery (CNC lathe with sparks, Ullage hypergolic engine, Veggie hydroponic chamber, spectrometer, and holographic table) are mathematically drawn in real time on an 800×600 pixel HTML5 <canvas>, complemented by an active star minimap (240×120) and dynamic avatars.
  • Calibration Based on Real Physical Parameters: When interacting with a malfunctioning machine, a panel with sliders appears where the player must adjust two technical variables within a +/- 5 tolerance range relative to the nominal value used in space missions (e.g., cabin pressure at 14.7 psi, airflow at 45 CFM, LEO orbital altitude at 400 km with an inclination of 51.6°, or TDRS satellite link frequency in Ku-band at 15.0 GHz). Each parameter includes a scientific explanation of why that value is critical in microgravity.
  • Collision Detection and Progression: It uses bounding box collision detection (AABB) for station navigation, proximity triggers for interacting with objects or crew members, and a status system that evaluates the completion of daily tasks before allowing progression to the next orbital cycle via the sleep pod.
  • Multiplatform and Bilingual Adaptability: Allows real-time switching between Spanish and English and offers dedicated modes for PC (WASD/Arrow keys, Spacebar, and mouse) and mobile (directional pad and on-screen touch action button), in addition to including a recreational Ping Pong minigame in the crew quarters.

What are the benefits?

  • Applied and Contextualized STEM Learning: Transforms abstract principles of physics, chemistry, robotics, and aerospace engineering—such as water electrolysis (OGS), friction welding in a vacuum, Newton's Third Law in extravehicular activity (EVA), and infrared spectroscopy—into practical decisions with immediate feedback.
  • Decision-Making Under Real Constraints: Trains critical thinking by forcing the user to balance real engineering trade-offs (economic cost versus payload mass and launcher capacity) and to prioritize tasks during timed emergencies.
  • Universal Accessibility Without Technical Barriers: Running natively in the browser without requiring downloads, installations, or dedicated graphics cards, it works smoothly on both low-resource school computers and smartphones.
  • International Educational Reach: Thanks to its integrated real-time translation between Spanish and English, it can be used seamlessly in bilingual classrooms, science outreach workshops, and international competitions.

What do you hope to achieve?

  • Inspire Aerospace and STEM Careers: Bring space engineering closer to students and the general public through an engaging experience that illustrates how spacecraft systems keep crews alive and enable the study of worlds beyond our solar system.
  • Demonstrate the Potential of Open Web Standards: Prove that complex, visually rich, cross-platform educational simulators can be built using pure web technologies without relying on heavy game engines.
  • Evolve Into a Modular Educational Platform: Expand the simulator in future iterations with telemetry based on open NASA exoplanet catalogs, new extravehicular repair scenarios, and performance analytics for educators and science clubs.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Programming Languages: HTML5 (interface layers and modal structures), CSS3 (custom animations, emergency alert keyframes, and responsive layout), and JavaScript ES6+ (game engine, AABB collision physics, state machine, mission logic, launch simulator, and procedural vector rendering).
  • APIs, Frameworks, and Libraries: HTML5 Canvas 2D API (native procedural graphics engine), Tailwind CSS (responsive HUD and calibration modals), SoundCloud Widget API (looping 16-bit arcade soundtrack and volume control), and Google Fonts (Rajdhani and Inter).
  • Software and Hardware: Source code editor and modern web browsers with Developer Tools (DevTools) for real-time debugging, 60 FPS optimization, and mobile viewport emulation, tested on both desktop PCs and touchscreen smartphones
